articles.title: Google could be working on an incognito upgrade for Gemini Live
articles.excerpt: Because not everything you show to Gemini is something you want it to remember.
articles.body: TL;DR Google appears to be developing an “Ephemeral Video Mode” for Gemini Live. It’s possible that this could essentially let you go incognito for a Live session, while still working with video input. Normally, video shared with Live is archived in your Gemini Apps Activity. Not every interaction we have with AI needs to take place under the same constraints — and well-designed systems will give us the control we need to dial that in, just how we want it. Sometimes, privacy is going to be paramount, and we want the AI forgetting about the whole interaction the second it’s over. Other times, context is everything, and we want the AI remembering everything for future sessions.

articles.body: A customer opens their dashboard and sees another company’s invoices. Nobody needed to break in. An endpoint returned data it should never have returned. That’s one of the mistakes I want to make harder to introduce when building a B2B SaaS. Authentication alone doesn’t solve it: a user can be correctly logged in and still receive another customer’s data. For BootSaaS , I chose a schema-per-tenant architecture with Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, and Liquibase. I want separate business tables for each customer, a shared connection budget, and deployments a small team can operate. For that combination, schema-per-tenant is my clear choice. This is an architecture walkthrough. The examples illustrate the design rather than provide a complete implementation. First, what counts as a tenant?

articles.title: Crystal memory: notes that arrive when you act, not when you go looking
articles.excerpt: Sixty days in we still cannot prove it helped, so we started hiding it from ourselves at random to find out. A note in our system carries a line that says, in effect, "show me when somebody is about t…
articles.body: Sixty days in we still cannot prove it helped, so we started hiding it from ourselves at random to find out. What it does A note in our system carries a line that says, in effect, "show me when somebody is about to run a command that looks like this." Nobody searches for it. When the agent is about to run a shell command, write a file, or make a commit, the notes bound to that action arrive in its context right then. We call the notes crystals, and the whole thing crystal memory. The name is the most fanciful part of it. Everything underneath is four files of plain Python and a rule about when a note is allowed to speak. Here is a real one, and it is in the free starter set because we hit it ourselves.

articles.title: A task-healer has to bound its own coordination noise
articles.excerpt: On 2026-09-16 we measured a failure mode in the mesh task healer: resolver-for-resolver ~/.mesh/evidence/unblock-mess-20260916/inventory.md counted 627 unique unblock steps; 275 were unblock/... task,…
articles.body: On 2026-09-16 we measured a failure mode in the mesh task healer: resolver-for-resolver retries were producing coordination noise faster than they produced recovery. The inventory at ~/.mesh/evidence/unblock-mess-20260916/inventory.md counted 627 unique unblock steps; 275 were meta-steps whose blocker was itself another unblock/... task, and 95 of those were still open, active, or blocked. The deepest observed ancestry was four levels. The implementation now caps resolver-for-resolver [yield] emissions at three per sweep, then posts one roll-up and parks further overflow in the sweep log. Per-chain marks remain available, so the cap reduces board volume without deleting retry provenance.

articles.title: Survey reveals where most of you draw the line when it comes to AI
articles.excerpt: Our reader poll put LLM trust to the test by asking whether you'd hand an agent full access to your computer.
articles.body: Credit: Adamya Sharma / Android Authority LLMs have only been on the scene for a few years, but for better or worse, they’ve long since escaped the chat window. Instead of just answering questions or rewriting your emails, the next wave of AI agents wants to do most of the clicking for you, but this generally requires getting its hands on much more of your computer. We can probably all agree that this could save you a lot of tedious work, but it also means handing a somewhat unpredictable machine the digital equivalent of your house keys. We wanted to know if you were cool with that. That trade-off came into focus when we tried OpenClaw earlier this year, an open-source tool that effectively lets an LLM work directly with your computer and connected services.

articles.body: TL;DR Google is expanding CC from a personal daily briefing tool into an AI assistant for families and households. Up to six people can share information with CC, which can manage shared calendars, tasks, reminders, and Daily Briefs. CC can also help with chores like filling out forms, making shopping lists, and planning meals. Late last year, Google introduced an all-new attempt at making Gemini a lot more useful for everyday life. Called CC, it was a new AI agent designed to give you a daily briefing and help you follow up on tasks by tracking information found within your Gmail, Calendar, and Drive. The Google Labs experiment evolved into Gemini’s Daily Brief , and Google is now taking the original CC concept and expanding its horizon.

Although the orbiter was originally planned to be named Constitution, Star Trek fans successfully convinced President Gerald Ford to name it Enterprise after the series’ fictional starship. NASA Fifty years ago, on Sept. 17, 1976—Constitution Day of America’s bicentennial year—NASA unveiled its first space shuttle orbiter, OV-101, to the public. NASA had originally planned to name the vehicle Constitution, but a letter-writing campaign changed the agency’s plans. Nearly 100,000 fans of the Star Trek television series wrote the White House urging that the shuttle be named after the USS Enterprise, the fictional starship featured in the series.

As you’re no doubt aware, the biggest story in tech right now is the spiraling debate about AI safety and regulation.  It should come as no surprise that Mustafa has strong opinions on how AI should be built and regulated. Microsoft just published a 37-page statement called the “Humanist AI Code of Conduct,” which lays out the company’s principles around AI development and even its philosophy around really thorny issues like AI consciousness.  If you’ll recall from his last appearance on the show, Mustafa thinks companies like Anthropic have gotten really confused about this concept of so-called model welfare in fairly dangerous ways.
